title: The Instrumental and the Vocative
summary: The last two cases, and with them the whole declension. The instrumental says with what a thing is done, in whose company, and at what recurring time; the vocative does nothing but call a person by name.

rules.heading: The Instrumental Singular
rules.statement: The **instrumental** answers *kuo?* (with what? by what means?). Its singular endings are given below. Two of them deserve warning: the feminine **-a** declension has an instrumental spelled exactly like its nominative — *knyga* is both — and the masculine **-us** declension takes the long ending **-umi**, not the short *-u* of the other masculines.

paradigms.caption: Nominative → instrumental singular
paradigms.footnote: The feminine *knyga → knyga* is a genuine homograph, distinguished in speech by tone and in writing by nothing at all; the sentence must settle it, and it always does, because a nominative and an instrumental never do the same work.

examples.gloss: I am writing with a pencil.
I am eating with a spoon.

rules.heading: The Dative and Instrumental Plural
rules.statement: The two cases are best learnt together in the plural, because their endings run in parallel: where the dative has **-ms**, the instrumental has **-is** or **-mis**. With these the declension is complete — every one of the seven cases has now been given in both numbers.

paradigms.caption: Dative and instrumental plural
paradigms.footnote: Adjectives take the same endings and agree as always: *geriems draugams*, to good friends; *gerais žodžiais*, with good words.

examples.gloss: I am writing to my friends.

examples.note: plural where English keeps the singular, because more than one journey is meant

rules.heading: The Instrumental of Means
rules.statement: The commonest use of the case, and the one that names it: the **thing by which** an action is performed stands in the instrumental, with **no preposition**. English needs *with* or *by*; Lithuanian needs only the ending, and adding a preposition where none belongs is the error to guard against.

examples.gloss: I go to work by bicycle.

examples.target: Ji valgo šaukštu, o ne peiliu.
examples.gloss: She eats with a spoon, not with a knife.

footnotes: Do not say *su pieštuku* for "with a pencil": *su* is for company, not for tools (¶74).

rules.heading: Company: Su and the Instrumental
rules.statement: **Su** governs the instrumental and means *together with* — in somebody's company, or with something added to something else. It is the difference between the tool and the companion: one writes *pieštuku*, with a pencil, but goes *su draugu*, with a friend. Coffee **su pienu** is coffee with milk added, and the same preposition serves.

rules.heading: Po with the Instrumental, and Po with the Genitive
rules.statement: **Po** is two prepositions wearing one spelling, and the case tells them apart. With the **instrumental** it is *under*, of place; with the **genitive** it is *after*, of time (¶33). Nothing but the ending distinguishes them, which is why a preposition must always be learnt together with the case it governs.

examples.gloss: The book is under the table.
The cat is sleeping under the bed.

rules.heading: The Instrumental of Recurring Time and of Route
rules.statement: Two further uses, both idiomatic and both frequent. A **plural** instrumental of a time-word means *on such days as a rule* — not one Monday but Mondays in general. And the surface **along which** motion happens stands in the instrumental too, where English says *along* or *down*.

paradigms.caption: Recurring time
paradigms.footnote: A single occasion is not put here but in the accusative — *pirmadienį*, on Monday — which ¶83 will give with the rest of the ways of saying when.

examples.gloss: At weekends we do not work.
In the evenings I read books.

rules.heading: Verbs Governing the Instrumental
rules.statement: A few verbs take the instrumental as their only object, and one of them is needed the first time a learner falls ill. **Sirgti**, to be ill, asks *kuo?* — one is ill *with* an illness, never *an* illness. **Kvėpuoti**, to breathe, does the same.

examples.note: literally: with what are you ill

examples.gloss: The child has a throat infection.

rules.heading: The Vocative
rules.statement: The **vocative** is the case of address: it names the person spoken to and takes no part in the grammar of the sentence, which is why it is set off by a comma. It has no plural of its own — the nominative plural serves — and its singular endings are these. A few common exceptions must simply be known: names in *-as* take **-ai**, agent nouns in *-ėjas, -ojas* take **-au**, and familiar words in *-ukas* drop the ending altogether.

paradigms.caption: Nominative → vocative singular
paradigms.footnote: The feminine *-a* words are unchanged, so *mama* is both nominative and vocative — as *knyga* was both nominative and instrumental in ¶71. Lithuanian tolerates such coincidences because the sentence never leaves both readings open.

examples.note: *ponas* → *pone*, and the title follows into the vocative

vocabulary.gloss: with, in the company of (+ instr.)

vocabulary.notes: The illness stands in the instrumental: sergu gripu.

drills.stem: What is the instrumental singular of **sūnus**?
drills.explanation: The **-us** class takes long **-umi**, not bare *-u* (¶71). *sūnui* is dative; *sūnuje* locative; *sūnu* is the false analogy from *namu*.

drills.stem: Complete: **Rašau ____.** (I am writing with a pencil.)
drills.explanation: Means take a **bare** instrumental — no preposition (¶73). *su pieštuku* makes the pencil a companion (¶74); accusative/genitive do not belong.

drills.stem: How do you address **Eglė**?
drills.explanation: Feminine **-ė** → vocative **-e**: *Labas, Egle!* *Eglei* is dative; *Eglės* genitive.

drills.stem: **Knyga po stalu** vs **Po pietų dirbu** — what distinguishes them?
options: The first is wrong; place needs *ant*.
drills.explanation: Same spelling, two prepositions: instrumental → place "under"; genitive → time "after" (¶75).

drills.stem: Which are **correct**?
drills.explanation: *su* is company or addition (friend; milk in coffee). Pencil and bus are **means** → bare instrumental: *rašau pieštuku*, *važiuoju autobusu*. English *with/by* tempts the extra *su*.

drills.stem: Complete: **Aš sergu ____.** (I have flu.)
drills.explanation: *sirgti* governs bare instrumental: *sergu gripu* (¶77). Accusative *gripą* is the English-transfer error; *su* is for company, not illness.

drills.stem: What is the dative plural of **katė**?
drills.explanation: Dative plural **-ms** vs instrumental plural **-mis**: *katėms* / *katėmis*. The others are locatives.

drills.stem: Which **mokytojas** forms are correctly matched?
drills.explanation: Agent *-ojas* takes vocative **-au**, not *-ai*. *mokytojams* is **dative** plural; instrumental plural is *mokytojais*.

drills.stem: **Savaitgaliais mes nedirbame.** Why is *savaitgaliais* plural instrumental?
options: Because the instrumental has no singular.
Because plural instrumental of a time-word means the occasion as a rule, not once.
Because *mes* is plural and the time-word agrees with it.
drills.explanation: *savaitgaliais* = weekends in general (¶76). One weekend would be accusative *savaitgalį*. Time-words do not agree with the subject.

drills.stem: Feminine *knyga* is identical in nominative and instrumental singular. How is the reading settled?
options: By an accent mark in ordinary print.
By the sentence: nominative and instrumental never do the same job.
drills.explanation: A genuine homograph (¶71): tone may differ in speech, writing shows nothing — syntax decides (*Knyga yra nauja* vs *Rašau knyga* would be odd; means usually *pieštuku*-type words).

drills.stem: Counting both numbers, how many case×number **slots** does the full seven-case declension comprise?
drills.explanation: Seven cases × two numbers = 14 slots (¶72). Vocative plural borrows nominative shape, so fewer distinct spellings appear — the question asks for slots.

drills.stem: Which numbered rule of this section governs the form used to address someone directly? Give the paragraph number.
drills.explanation: ¶78 sets out the vocative. The near miss is ¶71, the instrumental singular, which shares the section but not the function.

drills.stem: Instrumental singular of **pieštukas**?
drills.explanation: *-as* → **-u**: *pieštuku* (¶71). *pieštukui* is dative.

drills.stem: Complete: **Rašau ____.**
drills.explanation: Means = bare instrumental (¶73). *su pieštuku* would treat the pencil as company.

drills.stem: Vocative of **mokytojas**?
drills.explanation: Address form **-au**: *mokytojau* (¶78).

drills.stem: Complete: **Einu ____ draugu.** (I am going with a friend.)
drills.explanation: Company = **su** + instrumental (¶74).

drills.stem: Complete: **Į darbą važiuoju ____.** (I go to work by bicycle.)
drills.explanation: Vehicle as means = bare instrumental *dviračiu* (¶73). *su* would mean 'together with a bicycle' as companion.

drills.stem: Complete: **Aš sergu ____.** (I have flu.)
drills.explanation: *sirgti* takes instrumental of the illness: *gripu* (¶77).

drills.stem: Which correctly use **su** vs bare instrumental?
drills.explanation: *su* is company/addition; pencil and bus are means → bare instrumental. *Rašau su pieštuku* is the near-miss (¶73–74).

drills.stem: Which express **habitual time** with plural instrumental?
drills.explanation: Plural instrumental = 'on such days as a rule' (¶76). *Pirmadienį* is one Monday (accusative of time).

drills.stem: **Knyga po stalu** vs **Po pietų dirbu**. What distinguishes the two *po*?
drills.explanation: *po* + instrumental = under; *po* + genitive = after (¶75).

drills.stem: Dative plural of **draugas**?
drills.explanation: Dative plural **-ams**: *draugams* (¶72). *draugais* is instrumental plural.

drills.stem: Which vocatives are **correct**?
drills.explanation: Vocative reshapes the name: *Egle*, *mokytojau*, *Vytautai*. Nominative *Eglė* in address is the near-miss (¶78).

drills.stem: Complete: **Arbata ____ citrina.** (Tea with lemon.)
drills.explanation: Addition/company with *su* + instrumental: *su citrina* (¶74).

drills.stem: Which of these mark **company** with *su*, not bare means?
drills.explanation: *su mama* and *su draugu* are company. *pieštuku* and *autobusu* are bare instrumental of means.

drills.stem: Letters in instrumental **sūnumi**?
drills.explanation: Seven: s-ū-n-u-m-i. *-us* class takes long **-umi** (¶71).

drills.stem: In **Rašau draugams ir seserims**, how many words stand in the dative plural?
drills.explanation: *draugams* and *seserims* are both dative plurals, in *-ams* and *-ims* according to declension (¶72). *Rašau* is the verb and *ir* a conjunction, so neither stands in a case at all.

drills.title: Rytas su Vytautu
drills.passage: Vytautas gyvena su broliu. Savaitgaliais jie nedirba, bet šiandien pirmadienis. Rytais Vytautas važiuoja į darbą dviračiu, o brolis — autobusu. Šiandien brolis serga gripu ir guli lovoje. Jis klausia: „Vytautai, ar turi vandens?“ Vytautas duoda broliui vandens ir važiuoja į darbą vienas. Jis rašo pieštuku, ne ranka.
drills.translation: Vytautas lives with his brother. At weekends they do not work, but today is Monday. In the mornings Vytautas goes to work by bicycle, and his brother by bus. Today the brother is ill with flu and is lying in bed. He asks: "Vytautas, have you got some water?" Vytautas gives his brother some water and goes to work alone. He writes with a pencil, not by hand.

questions.explanation: *Rytais Vytautas važiuoja į darbą dviračiu, o brolis — autobusu.* The bare instrumental names the means, and the dash stands in for the repeated verb.

questions.stem: Kodėl brolis šiandien neina į darbą?
questions.explanation: *Šiandien brolis serga gripu ir guli lovoje.* The passage says plainly that today is Monday, so the weekend is ruled out by the text itself.
*važiuoja … dviračiu* — the bus is the brother's. *kuo?* asks exactly for the instrumental of means.
*su broliu* company; *savaitgaliais* recurring time; *gripu* object of *sirgti*. *broliui* is dative — the recipient of water.

questions.stem: Count the words in the passage that stand in the **vocative**.
questions.explanation: One: the person addressed by name. Every other noun in the passage is doing a job in the sentence — subject, object or complement — and only direct address takes the vocative (¶78).

questions.stem: **Jis rašo pieštuku, ne ranka.** Why no *su* before *pieštuku*?
options: Because a tool/means takes bare instrumental; *su* would mark company.
questions.explanation: Means vs company is the whole point of ¶73–¶74: *pieštuku* / *ranka* bare; *su broliu* for a person.
*gripu* is the object of *sirgti* (illness in instrumental), not a tool of means. The other three are textbook means/company contrasts.
